confidence_note: DB lists the title only as the Turkish 'Zengin Baba Fakir Baba'; English title used. Written from well-known content (memory plus summaries), book text not opened. Old TR text errors: it says his own father was a 'retired civil servant whose pay stopped at retirement' and rich dad was 'a neighbour' and that Kiyosaki calls the cycle a 'hamster wheel'. In the book the poor dad (his real father) holds a Ph.D. and heads Hawaii's department of education, then resigns to run for lieutenant governor, loses and is out of work; rich dad is the father of his friend Mike and left school early; Kiyosaki's phrase is 'rat race', not 'hamster wheel'. Omitted: exact ages and years, the 10-cents-an-hour episode, the claim about the house's status (kept for the lesson-free part). Ten-cents-an-hour store episode: medium confidence on the wage, age and Rich Dad's response (remembered from the book, not re-checked).
facts: Kiyosaki grew up with two fathers: his own, whom the book calls Poor Dad, and the father of his best friend Mike, Rich Dad.
Poor Dad held a Ph.D. and ran Hawaii's state education system; Rich Dad left school early and built a business empire in Hawaii.
Poor Dad's advice: go to school, get good grades, find a safe job.
At about nine, Kiyosaki and Mike worked in Rich Dad's store for ten cents an hour; Kiyosaki complained about the pay and Rich Dad did not raise it.
Poor Dad held that the love of money is the root of all evil; Rich Dad held that the lack of money is.
When something cost too much, Poor Dad said 'I can't afford it'. Rich Dad banned that phrase in his home and asked 'How can I afford it?' instead.
Poor Dad resigned from his state job to run for lieutenant governor, lost, and found himself out of work. Rich Dad became one of the richest men in Hawaii.
Kiyosaki's summary: the poor and middle class work for money; the rich make money work for them.
scene_details: A father with a Ph.D. running the state's schools and a friend's father who left school early
The two phrases: 'I can't afford it' and 'How can I afford it?'
A resignation letter to run for office, followed by an election loss
tension: Two men the author trusted gave him opposite answers about money, and only one had finished school.
opening_idea: Open on the two fathers side by side: the Ph.D. who ran the schools and the friend's father who had left school.

lessons.idea: Replacing 'I can't afford it' with a question forces you to look for the route rather than closing the topic.
lessons.anchor: Rich Dad banned 'I can't afford it' and asked how he could afford it.
lessons.everyday_example_idea: A shop owner stuck on a costly repair asks what could pay for it instead of saying no.

reflect_final: Which purchase or plan have you dismissed with 'I can't afford it' that you could still rework into a question about how?

use_cases.situation: A teammate rejects a proposal for cost.
use_cases.move: Rich Dad asked 'How can I afford it?'; ask the team what would have to be true for it to be affordable.

use_cases.situation: Your child asks for something expensive.
use_cases.move: Skip the flat no and ask how they could earn or save part of it.

use_cases.situation: You catch yourself dropping a goal for money reasons.
use_cases.move: Write the goal and one way, however slow, it could be paid for.

pocket_idea: Rich Dad banned 'I can't afford it' in his house, because 'How can I afford it?' makes the mind search.

conversation_variants.punchline_idea: Kiyosaki's rich dad banned one sentence at home: 'I can't afford it'.
conversation_variants.thirty_sec_idea: Kiyosaki had two fathers, one with a Ph.D. who ran Hawaii's schools and one, his best friend's dad, who left school early. The first said get good grades and a safe job. The second banned 'I can't afford it' and asked 'How can I afford it?' The first lost an election and was out of work, the second grew rich.
